items.title: User name with a trailing space signs in as alice
covers: What should happen: alice followed by a space with the right password signs in as alice
items.reason: This is the exact reproduction in the ticket (a pasted name with a space after it) and the core of the fix; if it regresses the shopper is told their credentials are wrong. It needs the e2e layer because Identity.API has no in-process test project and the result is only visible as a completed sign-in round trip back to the WebApp.

items.title: User name with a leading space signs in as alice
covers: What should happen: a space followed by alice with the right password signs in as alice
What happens: the same happens with a space before the name
items.reason: The ticket names the leading-space variant separately as a failing input; a fix that only strips the end (`TrimEnd`) would pass TC-BUG-58-01 and still fail here, so it needs its own case. Same e2e reasoning as TC-BUG-58-01.

items.title: User name with spaces on both sides signs in as alice
covers: What should happen: spaces before or after the user name are ignored
items.reason: The rule is "spaces before or after the user name are ignored", plural; a name with several spaces on both sides is the literal combination of both reported variants and guards against a fix that strips only a single character or only one side. e2e for the same reason as TC-BUG-58-01.

items.title: The exact user name still signs in as alice
covers: What happens: with `alice` and the same password, signing in works
What should happen: exactly as `alice` does
items.reason: The ticket states that `alice` signs in today and is the reference behaviour the spaced names must match; the change touches the user name on every sign-in, so the unspaced path must not regress. e2e because it is the same round trip as TC-BUG-58-01 and is the baseline the spaced cases are compared with.

items.title: A spaced user name with a wrong password is still refused
covers: What should happen: a wrong password is still refused as today
items.reason: The ticket keeps the refusal of a wrong password; ignoring spaces must not turn into a looser credential check (for example matching the name and skipping the password). Using a spaced name proves the trimmed name still goes through the password check. Uses `bob` with a single failed attempt so the lockout-on-failure counter never locks `alice`, whom the happy cases use.

items.title: A spaced unknown user name with a valid password is still refused
covers: What should happen: a wrong user name is still refused as today
items.reason: The ticket keeps the refusal of a wrong user name; trimming must not make an unknown name match an existing account. The password is a real one (`bob`'s) so the only wrong thing is the user name. No account is touched, so the lockout counter is not involved.

items.file: TC-BUG-58-01..04 Expected result; story 'What should happen'
items.reason: The ticket says `alice ` and ` alice` 'sign in as alice'. The expected results (and those of TC-02, TC-03 and TC-04) only check that the Account button replaces Sign in, which proves someone is signed in but not who. Add to each happy case: open the Account menu and assert that `.user-menu-name` (src/WebApp/Components/Layout/UserMenu.razor:15, User.Identity.Name) shows alice's name, the same text TC-04's plain `alice` sign-in shows, so the spaced sign-ins are proven identical to it ('exactly as alice does').

Redirecting to WebApp and showing Account proves authentication but does not establish that the authenticated account is alice. Extend the success cases to observe the authenticated username or subject through a public UI or HTTP interface and compare it with seeded alice.
